summary: Reports on an Internet Architecture Board workshop in October 2006 in Amsterdam on routing and addressing. Its aim was a shared understanding of the routing scalability problems that large backbone operators face. Findings cover what drives routing table growth, router technology limits, and limits of the addressing architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts met to figure out why the internet's directions book was getting too big and what could be done about it.

subtitle: What large network operators told the IAB about why the Internet routing table keeps growing, and what any fix must achieve.

tldr.problem: The Default Free Zone (DFZ) routing table was growing fast, driven by multihoming, traffic engineering and unaggregatable address allocations, while router hardware was getting costlier to scale.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a workshop on October 18-19, 2006 in Amsterdam with large backbone operators and router vendors. It produced a prioritized problem statement, solution criteria and recommendations.
tldr.outcome: The workshop named routing scalability and the overloading of IP addresses as both locator and identifier as the two top problems, and asked the IAB and IESG to lead the next steps. The report states that the views are those of the participants, not the IAB.

today: RFC 4984 is an Informational report that has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata. It records the participants' views as of 2006 and itself says that work on these issues was continuing.

sections.title: Why the IAB Held the Workshop
sections.content:
This memo is a report on a Routing and Addressing Workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on October 18-19, 2006, in Amsterdam. Its main goal was a shared understanding of the scaling problems that large backbone operators face with today's routing system.

The report is not an official IAB document. The views in it are those of the workshop participants, who were mostly large network operators and a few router vendors. The report itself notes that a different group, such as end users and enterprise operators, would likely produce a different list of priorities, for example putting freedom to change providers without renumbering near the top.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of people who run big parts of the internet got together to write down what is going wrong with its address book, so others could start fixing it.

sections.title: The Two Top Problems
sections.content:
The participants ranked two problems highest. Problem 1 is the scalability of the routing system: the size of the DFZ routing table (the RIB) and the forwarding table built from it (the FIB), plus the cost of recomputing the FIB, BGP convergence times, and the cost and power of core router hardware.

The main drivers of RIB growth were multihoming, traffic engineering, non-aggregatable address allocations (much of it inherited from history) and business events such as mergers. All of them can cause prefix de-aggregation, which also raises the number of BGP UPDATE messages ("UPDATE churn") that the core must handle. The report puts the DFZ at about 200,000 entries as of October 2006 and cites a projection of 370,000 or more within 5 years.

Problem 2 is the overloading of IP address semantics. An address says both who a host is (an identifier, used by transport) and where it is (a locator, used by routing). The report argues that one number space cannot serve both purposes efficiently, so a locator/identifier split seems necessary. How to build such a split was not explored in detail.

Rekhter's Law, quoted in the report: addressing can follow topology, or topology can follow addressing. Choose one.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a phone book where every house keeps its old number even when it moves, so the book keeps getting fatter. The workshop said the book is growing too fast, and that an address is trying to be both a name and a street location at once.

sections.title: What Drives Routing Table Growth
sections.content:
Much of the growth comes from de-aggregation, where operators advertise more-specific prefixes on purpose. The report lists three pressures.

  • Avoiding renumbering: customers prefer provider-independent (PI) space. Renumbering is hard because addresses are baked into access control lists and sometimes hard-coded into applications. Regional registries allocate PI prefixes to customers who claim a need, and ISPs do not typically charge to route them.
  • Multihoming: a site served by more than one ISP. If a customer's provider-allocated prefix is advertised by a non-primary ISP, longest-prefix matching pulls traffic that way, and the primary ISP must de-aggregate the prefix to keep the traffic.
  • Traffic engineering (TE): steering traffic onto chosen paths, usually done by splitting prefixes. It helps the operator who does it, but raises the cost for the whole Internet.

This is the misaligned costs and benefits problem: the party that gains from an extra route does not bear the cost of carrying it. For IPv6, a full immediate transition is estimated to grow RIB and FIB sizes by a factor of about four, and the report warns of an unaggregatable "swamp" many orders of magnitude larger than IPv4's.
sections.plainLanguage: Every time a family wants its own special mailbox number that follows them around, the post office has to write one more line in its big book. Everyone benefits a little, but the post office pays for the thicker book.

sections.title: Router Hardware and Moore's Law
sections.content:
A common hope is that Moore's Law will keep hardware ahead of table growth. A workshop presentation by Tony Li argued otherwise for core routers. Moore's Law comes from the high-volume chip industry, while the custom silicon in core routers is made in far lower volume, typically 1,000-10,000 parts per year, so it does not inherit the same cost curve.

The report gives several constraints. DRAM capacity grows faster than Moore's Law would suggest, but DRAM speed only grows about 10% per year, and BGP convergence is limited by DRAM access speed. Off-chip SRAM, favored for FIBs, is no longer a volume part. Tapeout costs have been rising about 1.5x every 2 years. Heat and power are also limits, and air cooling is starting to limit high-performance routers.

The summary figure is a sustainable growth rate of 1.3x per 2 years for the forwarding table and 1.2x per 2 years for the routing table. The report says the baseline growth was already 1.3x per 2 years, with bursts that exceeded Moore's Law, so the cost of technology refresh keeps growing. The report adds editor's notes that this section drew debate after the workshop and needs further community input.
sections.plainLanguage: People hoped computers would just keep getting cheaper fast enough to hold the growing book. But the special parts big routers need are made in small numbers, so they do not get cheap as quickly.

sections.title: Approaches Reviewed
sections.content:
The workshop looked at earlier work. The MULTI6 working group found that changing current practice is hard, and that IP addresses are hard-coded as identifiers in applications and network policies.

SHIM6 is host-based: a shim layer presents a stable upper layer identifier (ULID) to upper protocols and rewrites packets to use a working address. That lets a multihomed site use provider-allocated prefixes, but it needs changes to all host stacks, gives providers little traffic engineering control, adds state on busy servers, and still forces renumbering when a site changes providers.

GSE splits the 16-byte IPv6 address so that the last 8 bytes identify an interface, while border routers rewrite the routing part. Map-and-Encap (RFC 1955) uses tunneling instead. Both need a mapping service from identifier to locators. That service adds complexity, another point of failure and a possible target for attack, but this class of approach needs no changes to end systems when border routers do the encapsulation. The report says it deserves special attention.
sections.plainLanguage: People tried a few tricks, like giving each computer a second address or putting letters in envelopes with a new outer label. Each trick helped one problem but made another job harder.

sections.title: Criteria and Recommendations
sections.content:
The workshop framed its solution constraints as criteria rather than hard rules. A solution should scale in DFZ routes and internal routes, treat scalable TE as a business necessity, align incentives so that practices that reduce overall cost are rewarded, and give benefits to first movers since there can be no flag day. It should work for both IPv4 and IPv6 and be backward compatible with BGP, OSPF and IS-IS, possibly with incremental enhancements. On timing, a 1-2 year specification plus a 2-year certification cycle means 3-5 years to deployment even in the best case. Security should be considered from day one, but securing the routing system was not considered a requirement.

The recommendations were:

  • Treat routing scalability as important and start a long-term solution.
  • Have the IAB and IESG reach out to other stakeholders such as content providers, retail providers and enterprise operators.
  • Develop the solution openly, with research community participation, with the IAB leading investigation of the locator-identifier split.
  • Consider short- or intermediate-term fixes to buy time, for example FIB compression.
  • Develop a roadmap with short-, medium- and long-term objectives.
sections.plainLanguage: The group said: start fixing this soon, ask everyone else what they need, do it in the open, and make a plan with small steps and big steps.

items.title: Multihoming
items.text: Sites served by more than one ISP often force their prefixes to be advertised separately.

items.title: Traffic engineering
items.text: Operators split prefixes to steer traffic onto chosen paths.

items.title: Non-aggregatable allocations
items.text: Much of this is inherited from historical address allocations.

items.title: Business events
items.text: Mergers and acquisitions can leave unaggregatable prefixes.
